title: 5 Ways to Start a Presentation
summary: The creator explains that most presenters lose their audience in the first thirty seconds by starting in a boring way. She shares five engaging ways to start a presentation to keep the audience listening.
key_points: Most presenters lose their audience in the first thirty seconds because they open in the safest, most forgettable, most boring way.

Five ways to start a presentation: 1. Start With a Surprising Statistic, 2. Start Immediately With Audience Interaction, 3. Lead With The Audience Outcome, 4. Start With a Story, 5. Use a Prop, Visual Tool or Activity.
Method 1: Start with a surprising statistic that immediately signals urgency, tension, or opportunity so people understand why it matters, the scale of the problem, and what is at stake.
Method 2: Start immediately with audience interaction by asking a question, such as a show of hands, typing in chat, or asking people around the room, to make them go into active mode.
Method 3: Lead with the audience outcome by focusing on the benefit the audience will have from listening to you, rather than explaining the topic itself.
Method 4: Start with a story because it immediately shifts people from analyzing business as usual to experiencing, and is one of the most efficient ways to communicate complex information.
Method 5: Use a prop, visual tool, or activity, which is very effective in virtual presentations where people are still joining the meeting and are distracted or mentally elsewhere.
The best presentations usually create one of the following: curiosity, emotion, participation, relevance, or tension.
content: The creator, Shannen Jenkins, marketing manager at Resonate, claims that the moment you start your presentation, you have the listeners' full attention. But most people do this: "Hello everyone, nice to see you so um, thanks thanks for being here just checking can can everyone can everyone hear me okay?" and then they add "just can everyone see me okay? I'm I'm just gonna wait for a few more people to join the call." And what happens? Audience pulls out their phone. You've lost them. Shannen has hosted stages with thousands of people at conferences like Startup Nights, Start Summit, Health Tech Global Summit, and trained hundreds of managers and leaders at organizations like Nestle, Nespresso, Google to deliver more impactful presentations. She shares the five ways to start a presentation so that people actually listen, engage, and resist the temptation to check their phones. Method 1: Start With a Surprising Statistic. A statistic that immediately signals either urgency, tension, or opportunity. A bad example: "Hi everyone, I'm Shannen Jenkins from digital strategy, head of digital transformation, and today I'll be talking to you about how we can optimize website efficiency across the business." Boring, dull. A good example: 40 million francs. That is how much we spend on websites every single year. It is far worse than the industry average and I am going to present a plan to make sure we can optimize and reduce that so we stay ahead as a business. People pay more attention when you signal urgency. Choose the most convincing piece of data and start there, because people understand immediately why it matters, the scale of the problem, and potentially what is at stake. Method 2: Start Immediately With Audience Interaction. The fastest way to increase engagement and reduce that problem of picking up the phone, checking email, multitasking, is to ask the audience a question. Make them go into active mode rather than passive. For in-person, ask for a show of hands. For virtual, ask people to type in the chat. For smaller meetings, ask people around the room directly. Method 3: Lead With The Audience Outcome. This is one of the biggest mistakes Shannen sees in coaching, and it is honestly one of the easiest fixes because most presenters explain the topic, but very few explain why the audience should care. Instead of introducing the subject you are going to talk about, you are going to introduce the benefit the audience will have from listening to you. For example, last year Shannen was invited to give a keynote presentation at Nestle in Barcelona on storytelling in business. Instead of walking up on stage in front of an unknown group of about 70 people and saying, "Hi, hello everyone, I'm Shannen Jenkins, thank you for being here, today I'm going to talk to you about storytelling," she walked on stage and opened with this: "There is one communication tool that will make people engage with you, increase your influence across the business, and make your message seven times more likely to be remembered. That tool is storytelling." Method 4: Start With a Story. This is one of the most powerful ways to open a presentation because stories immediately shift people from analyzing business as usual to experiencing. Contrary to what many professionals assume, storytelling isn't just entertainment or emotional fluff. Research actually suggests that storytelling is one of the most efficient ways to communicate complex information in a way that the brain can understand, remember, and act on. But most presenters make the mistake of opening with abstract corporate language, corporate blah blah, instead of something that's human and concrete. Method 5: Use a Prop, Visual Tool, or Activity. This is very, very effective in virtual presentations where people are still joining the meeting and they're either distracted, or they're mentally elsewhere, or they're checking their email and still doing some other work. Shannen encouraged one of her groups at Nestle to do this last year, and what was funny is that somebody came to me and they said, "Yeah, I I literally join a meeting about three to four minutes late on purpose, because I want to avoid that awkward start where people don't cut right into the meeting or the presentation and they do that exact thing like, oh just gonna wait, got thanks hi guys thanks for being here, I'm just I'm just gonna wait a couple of minutes for people to join." Don't do that. This is what when attention disappears and it also penalizes people who actually show up on time. So here's what you can do instead: you start your meeting with something visual, interactive, or unexpected. One real example of this: Shannen had a client working at innovation at Nespresso, and he expressed to his goal was to get the company to be more innovative, to have more creative thinking, and to think outside the box. Shannen asked him, "Are you familiar with that exercise where that terminology actually came from, of thinking outside the box?" He didn't know. But it came from this, the nine-dot puzzle. There's nine dots in a sequence here, and the challenge is that you have to connect all of these nine dots using four straight lines without lifting your pen off the paper. The solution to join those nine dots using only four straight lines is you have to go outside the box. So Shannen told this innovation manager, "Start your presentation like that, have your screen immediately shared on MS Teams, spotlight yourself so it shows up large, and then give people this challenge, and then you say what you're going to do in the presentation." He tested this out with his virtual presentation, there are about 25 people or so on the call, and some people grab their pen and paper, others started commenting on it in the chat, and it not only created curiosity, engagement, it also directly linked to the main message he wanted to share. The best presentations usually create one of the following: curiosity, emotion, participation, relevance, or tension.
